item.title: Some Introverts Think Best by Writing
item.description:
Introversion

Some Introverts Think Best by Writing

For some introverts, writing is thinking.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • For many introverts, writing isn't just a way to communicate ideas—it's how those ideas become clear.
  • Writing gives the brain time to question assumptions and organize complex thoughts.
  • Writing can help people arrive at more thoughtful conclusions than conversation alone often allows.
Source: Kristin Hardwick / StockSnap

It is easy to overlook those who are slowest to speak. Most of these are introverts. And some of those introverts, a rare but consequential minority, seem to most often experience thought most fully through the act of writing.

As Susan Cain (2012) observed, introversion spans a spectrum, united by a preference for low stimulation and rich reflection. Qualitative research reveals further nuance along that spectrum. For some, the internal monologue suffices; for others, thought develops and manifests best through writing, where words on a page are both a mirror and a lamp.

Writing as a Generator of Thought

The cognitive process theory of writing, as articulated by Flower and Hayes (1981), emphasized the recursive nature of it: writers do not simply transcribe ideas but generate and clarify them in the act of drafting itself.

Educational research shows that for some introverted students, writing jumpstarts thinking (Erickson et al., 2021).

Studies in primary education link higher writing performance and motivation to an interplay between unconscious rumination and purposeful, written exploration (Frontiers in Education, 2024). In this, the act of writing both reveals and refines what the mind knows and wants or needs to know.

Such findings resonate with my own experience. Time and again, insight emerges less from group discussion or even interior reflection than from hours spent articulating, revising, and distilling ideas through writing. The page absorbs the mind’s half-formed instincts and doubts, transforming chaos into clarity with an iterative patience few other mediums allow.

The Role of Reading, Motivation, and Emotional Regulation

This mode of thinking does not occur in a vacuum. Reading expands the mind’s lexicon and bank of ideas, as does, of course, the careful observation of the world around them that occurs as second nature and frequently from a slight distance.

Emotion also plays its part. Recent research highlights the importance of writing motivation—not simply the will to complete an assignment, but genuine interest, curiosity, and the freedom to select topics of relevance (Frontiers in Education, 2024).

For introverts, positive emotion and perceived self-efficacy can widen the doorway to creative risk and intellectual exploration, whereas pressure, ambivalence, or risk of external criticism may shutter it. In practical terms, creating private, low-stakes opportunities for writing can allow introverted individuals to find their stride.

article continues after advertisement
Source: Matt Moloney / StockSnap

Reflection, Critical Thinking, and the Slow Art of Revision

Writing is a slow art. Moon (1999) outlined how reflective writing deepens critical thinking and metacognition, inviting the writer to re-examine not just content, but process.

Evidence from educational settings indicates that brief but regular written reflection, even on familiar or non-technical subjects, can change the way students and professionals engage with material, developing both enduring interest and higher achievement (Erickson et al., 2021).

Reflection in writing, unlike speech, tolerates ambiguity, hesitation, and return. The writer can revisit an idea days or years later, layering new experiences atop old, and forming composites richer than either.

Psychologically, this recursive process mirrors internal growth.

Depth Over Speed

Observational and experimental research suggests that group projects and academic teams that include effective writing introverts often generate more nuanced solutions because their contributors excel at combing ideas for contradictions or possibilities (Shimek, 2023). Where conversation can orbit the surface of a problem, writing presses downward for coherence, demanding that claims and evidence align.

My own work with academic, leadership, operational, and clinical teams confirms that when introverted writers are given the space to submit written feedback, analysis, or proposals ahead of meetings, the total quality of group decision-making rises. Sometimes deliberation itself becomes slower, yet the substance and rigor of choices improve (Shimek, 2023).

article continues after advertisement
Source: Burst / StockSnap

The Value of the Writing Introvert

By pausing for deep consideration and daring to refine rather than rush, writing introverts often make durable contributions.

Team structures that build in asynchronous writing and reflection not only give introverted thinkers a voice but also improve group outcomes that can include richer solutions and stronger consensus (Frontiers in Education, 2024; Erickson et al., 2021). When such practices are carried into clinical, academic, or business domains, the “slow thinker” becomes quietly indispensable.

item.title: Why Lying Persists Despite the Consequences
item.description:
Deception

Why Lying Persists Despite the Consequences

How dissociation fuels both invention and deception across species.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Lying and falsehoods pose major problems in the criminal justice system, contributing to wrongful convictions.
  • Dissimulation and falsehood in the natural world promote survival in many species.
  • Dissociative factors in human psychology may contribute to dissimulation and its justification.
  • Understanding the dissociative psychological context of dissimulation may help to fight against it.
Source: Image by Matthew Sharps

Lying and falsehoods create a tremendous problem for the criminal justice system, resulting in large numbers of wrongful convictions (National Registry of Exonerations, 2025), despite the extreme legal consequences of perjury. The problem of dissimulation is significant in other areas, as well; the majority of people polled by the Pew Research Center believe that government communications and business advertising are filled with deliberately misleading or false information (Pew Research Center, 2025).

The Ubiquity of Falsehood Is Strange

Granted, the liar may gain a short-term advantage in any given case, but once you’re exposed as a liar, future victims would have to be awfully dissociated, psychologically, to believe you any further. Lies are frequently detected, presumably to the disadvantage of the liars. Why are humans so ready to dissimulate?

Falsehoods or the equivalent are ubiquitous in the natural world. For creatures that live moment to moment, falsehoods may prove entirely advantageous; dissimulation may have no long-term consequences, especially if those creatures and their conspecifics possess shorter or less sophisticated memories than their human counterparts. For example, some female fireflies give off mating signals to lure the males, after which they eat the males without a shred of the promised romance. Certain cuttlefish change their color and configuration to mimic females, preventing the need to fight or compete with larger males. These female impersonators swim right past their larger competitors to mate with available females while literally wearing false colors. A bird called the fork-tailed drongo, whose predator warning calls are heeded by other species of birds and mammals, which then fly or scurry away to escape, sometimes gives those calls when the other creatures are eating, causing them to flee their own meals. At that point, the “lying” drongos swoop in and scarf down the unearned meals (for example, Trecek-King, 2026). Dissimulation in the natural world depends, of course, on the physical and intellectual characteristics of the species in question, but it is found everywhere, in species as diverse as viruses and infrahuman primates (Trecek-King, 2026).

How a given creature lies depends on its physical nature and its normative ecology. If you're a cuttlefish, your chromatophores allow you to change color. If you're a drongo, you give alarm calls when there’s danger, but you can also squawk falsely but alarmingly whenever you want to scare hell out of the local meerkats and fly down to enjoy a meal of purloined bugs or maggots, once the original meerkat owners have fled in terror. And if you’re a human, you can lie via the gifts of language and dissociation.

article continues after advertisement

Human beings can use language to express truth, of course, but we can also dissociate our minds from physical reality to create false mental impressions, which we can then express linguistically. Even if we might get caught, we can lie, and we do.

Dissociation is a two-edged sword. In its most egregious forms, it can contribute to dissociative identity disorder; it can also convince us of “realities” that have no existence outside our own minds (Sharps and Price-Sharps, 2026). The positive side of dissociation, however, lies in our ability to imagine possibilities that don't yet exist, and then bring them into reality through our creative and inventive powers.

Unfortunately, a side effect of all the dissociative creativity means that we are also capable of lying like hell (Sharps, 2024; Sharps and Price-Sharps, 2026).

All of this might seem to provide some comforting justification for human falsehood. After all, lying in various forms is part of nature, so it must be okay; natural things are good, right?

Dissociation Again

As conventional religion has declined in many societies, beliefs in a benevolent nature may have become more prevalent and more influential (Sharps and Price-Sharps, 2026). Such beliefs originate more in the dissociative powers and properties of our minds than they do in the physical properties of nature itself, however. Nature does contain a great deal of that which the human species finds beautiful, true; but it also contains helpless maggots by the thousands who are horribly devoured by dissimulating drongos, or by cute little meerkats, who in turn die in screaming meerkat agony in the slavering jaws of hyenas, or poisoned painfully by puff adders, or crushed in the claws of screaming eagles. Granted, eagles are beautiful and majestic, at least when they’re not pecking bits of rotting meerkat out of their feathers, but the human constructions we place upon the natural world are the product of our minds, not of the entirely dispassionate reality of nature itself.

Dissociation, in more subtle and far less spectacular forms than we see in dissociative identity disorder, is essential to create the false pictures of reality with which we lie; but it is also essential to create the interpretations of the natural world which would enable us to justify our lies in some kind of weird kinship with the fork-tailed drongo (Sharps and Price-Sharps, 2026). Nature doesn’t justify anything. It just is.

article continues after advertisement

But because nature is, with a physical existence on which we depend for our survival, we can pay attention to it with as little dissociation involved as possible. One of the inescapable facts of nature today is the existence of over eight billion people on this single planet, all having to eat, survive, and cohabit while hopefully minimizing the carnage involved. Since lying and falsehood cause a lot of human conflict, it would therefore, with our current unprecedented world crowding, be a good idea to find psychological and cultural methods of reducing human dissimulation, across cultures, as much as possible. Unlike the drongos, we humans can explain lying in psychological terms; we might therefore be able to reduce it.

This is, of course, a naive, perhaps even a dissociated, proposition. However, unlike the drongos and the cuttlefish, humans can imagine possibilities that are not inherently immediate in our natures.

Let's hope we imagine, and perhaps even implement, the right ones.

item.title: Politician's Leave of Absence Highlights a Systemic Problem
item.description:
Depression

Politician's Leave of Absence Highlights a Systemic Problem

Serious inequities exist in how individuals secure mental health benefits.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • A recent news story reveals a staggering inequity in the accessibility of mental health leaves of absence.
  • For the layperson, securing mental health leave is a complicated and time-consuming process.
  • Fairness and accessibility of mental health benefits and accommodations is a nonpartisan issue.

For four months, New Jersey congressman Thomas Kean, Jr. was off the radar, missing 100 congressional votes. Constituents and media outlets did not know his whereabouts or why he had suddenly vanished. Recently, Congressman Kean revealed that he had been seeking treatment for depression, which had required him to take a four-month-long leave of absence. While we must continue to applaud those in the public eye for sharing their mental health struggles and for being transparent about serious issues like depression, we must also pay attention to discrepancies in how these types of accommodations are available to the general public versus to the elite and powerful.

The Excruciating Reality of Getting Leave

In my decade as a clinical social worker, I have helped many clients secure mental health-related benefits, in the form of the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) or through their companies’ human resources departments. In each case, the process is convoluted, difficult, frustrating, drawn out, and fraught with anxiety and stress. As an example, for an individual applying for mental health FMLA leave in the state of New Jersey, documentation is typically requested through postal mail, is often delayed in processing, and regularly requires multiple additional submissions or resubmissions. Of course, while this complex process is playing out, the individual’s mental health may continue to deteriorate.

Filing disability claims for mental health issues is by no means a sure thing; it can be difficult if not impossible to pinpoint when a specific mental health issue will subside, and so the types of questions that are often asked on application paperwork, such as “expected to end on…” or “anticipated return to work…,” can be tricky to answer. Receiving benefits for a physical health issue is by far easier than securing one for a mental health issue, despite the fact that both are essential for our survival. The reality for those individuals who are not in positions of power is that stepping away from work due to poor mental health is neither easy nor guaranteed. The story about Congressman Kean simply highlights this reality.

Inequities in Compensation

While Mr. Kean was away from Congress, he continued to receive his full salary and benefits. This is simply not the reality for the layperson; in fact, the process of attempting to receive compensation for a mental health leave is complicated. While FMLA guarantees job protection and unpaid leave, it does not compensate individuals for lost wages while away from work. In the state of New Jersey, a person seeking to be paid during leave must file for Temporary Disability Insurance, which, if approved, will compensate at 85% of the individual’s regular salary. Again, there is no guarantee that an individual will receive approval, and the application process itself is complicated and time-consuming. Mr. Kean was not required to go through any of this in order to secure his leave. This demonstrates a clear inequity between how those in power are treated during mental health crises and how those not in elite positions are treated.

article continues after advertisement

A Nonpartisan Issue

While Mr. Kean happens to be a member of the Republican Party, this is by no means a partisan issue; a Democrat or an Independent would have been afforded the same liberty to simply step away from work in order to seek treatment. In 2023, Democrats John Fetterman and Lina Hidalgo both took leaves to address clinical depression and likely did so while continuing to receive their full salaries. Taking politics out of the equation, the fact that mental health support and accommodations are often a class issue is at odds with the idea that we all deserve support regardless of social position. The recent news about Congressman Kane should remind us that mental health issues do not discriminate, and neither should we when we consider how to support those suffering from severe challenges like depression.

item.title: Accepting a Changing Body
item.description:
Body Image

Accepting a Changing Body

Strategies for cultivating a flexible body image.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • It is not only natural but also universal for our bodies to change over time.
  • We often believe and expect that our bodies will stay the same once we reach a certain point in adulthood.
  • This belief can increase insecurity or thinking we are unworthy in the face of a changing body.
  • You can practice skills to accept natural body changes and reduce the volume of self-criticism.
Source: dropthelabelmovement/unsplash

It is not only natural but also universal for our bodies to change over time. Body size and shape, and how our bodies function, change throughout adulthood. At different points in our adult lives, we may wear different clothing sizes and have varied physical abilities. For example, we experience a gradual loss of muscle mass as we age, starting in our 30s, and through middle age, fat naturally redistributes due to hormonal changes. Further, most adults gradually lose height starting in their 40s due to normal compression of the spine.

Yet, we often believe and expect that our bodies will stay the same once we reach a certain point in adulthood. This belief can make us feel insecure or lead us to think we are doing something wrong in the face of a changing body. In turn, we may criticize our changing bodies and ourselves, believing we are less worthy or valuable.

How do we practice accepting natural body changes and reducing the volume of self-criticism?

Cultivate a flexible body image

Rather than holding a rigid expectation that your body must stay the same over time, you can foster the ability to accept changes in your body by focusing on what it can do and how it helps you live your life, rather than on what it looks like. If you have experienced changes in your functional ability, acknowledge these changes, make space for the feelings you have (sadness, frustration, etc.), and allow yourself to grieve loss without judgment. At the same time, acknowledge that your body continues to do so much each day.

Normalize body changes and separate your sense of worth from your appearance

Many of us automatically talk to ourselves critically about our bodies based on ingrained beliefs and messages. It is important to shift unhelpful body self-talk by intentionally normalizing body changes and separating your sense of worth from your appearance via helpful self-talk. For example, saying to yourself, “Bodies change all the time. That is the rule, not the exception. This is normal, and my value is not based on how I look.”

You can also reinforce what you feel proud of yourself for that is not based on your looks by making a list of your non-appearance qualities and traits. Perhaps you are proud of your curiosity, open-mindedness, trustworthiness, or humor.

Stop trying to control your body

Are you exhausted by trying to control your body through methods such as dieting, over-exercising, or hypervigilance? How helpful have these methods been, not just related to maintaining a certain body size and shape, but also to your mood? Over time, do these methods help you feel more at ease and free, or do they lead you to feel more stress, anxiety, and self-criticism?

article continues after advertisement

Acknowledging and reflecting on how trying to control your body is unworkable and comes at a high cost to your mood and sense of vitality can open the door to acceptance of your body as it is and help you funnel your time and energy into more worthwhile and value-based pursuits.

Untangle your values from specific physical activities

Perhaps you are someone who walked an hour each day, and due to physical changes, can no longer do so. Or, you ran marathons and are no longer able to run. It can be emotionally challenging to let go of specific activities and goals, and it is helpful to untangle the activity from the value. What is values-based about your walk or run that is not based on the actual physical activity? Perhaps you value being outside, connecting with others who share a similar interest, or simply taking time for yourself without distraction.

Consider how your values can be honored within your current physical abilities. Just because a specific activity may not be doable, that does not mean you can’t continue to engage in values-based activities overall.

Focus on compassion, comfort, and confidence

Practice noticing when your self-critical internal voice arises and shift to repeating self-compassion statements. For example, “I am worthy as I am today” or “I am perfectly imperfect, and I accept myself as I am.”

article continues after advertisement

Focus on comfort and ease. What would help you feel comfortable and more at ease in your skin? Can you dress in comfortable clothing? Are there certain fabrics, textures, scents, etc., that you can put on your body that feel soothing?

Aim to feel confident as you are today. How can you feel confident and empowered in this moment? Is there music you can listen to, thoughts you can repeat, a certain piece of clothing or accessory you can wear, or an action you can take that allows you to feel confident, empowered, and strong as you are?

item.title: A Midlife Awakening: Seeing Things Anew in Our 50s and 60s
item.description:
Midlife

A Midlife Awakening: Seeing Things Anew in Our 50s and 60s

In midlife, some see things with fresh eyes, requiring a narrative revision.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • In midlife - after parents die, children leave, careers plateau - some people do an emotional audit.
  • Many find that the facts of their lives have not changed, but they often find the meaning has changed.
  • Such an awakening prompts a reorganization of relationships, purpose, and identity,
Source: Pexels/Jill Wellington

As I have coached clients in their struggles with siblings, I have found that many come to me in their 50s and 60s when they suddenly see themselves and their relationships from a fresh perspective.

These clients feel they have entered a new developmental life stage; it’s not a midlife crisis, with the classic signs of a fancy new car, an affair, or an obsession with changing one’s physical appearance.

It’s much more subtle. I would call it a midlife awakening.

The facts of their lives may not have changed, but they often find the meaning of their lives has. The awakening reveals itself in moments. Suddenly, a conversation with an adult child or sibling lands differently. A friendship that once felt fulfilling begins to feel one-sided. A marriage, a career, a family story no longer feels satisfying or a long-held belief no longer resonates as their perspective shifts. The awakening prompts a reorganization of relationships, purpose, and identity,

During a midlife awakening, many say that they feel like they have just come out of a long sleep. Adults at this stage do an emotional audit that is prompted by parents dying, children leaving, careers plateauing, and bodies changing. They look back over decades of relationships, obligations, triumphs, compromises, disappointments, and loyalties, and begin to see patterns that were harder to recognize while they were busy pressing through their days. The clock ticks louder than ever before. Truth-telling, forgiveness, grief, creativity, desire, and authenticity all feel more urgent.

Perhaps the best example of this shift in contemporary fiction may be what the character of Lucy Barton experiences in Elizabeth Strout’s work. Lucy's awakening is not a dramatic rupture, but a gradual dawning. As she looks back on her life of poverty, family silence, marriage, motherhood, artistic ambition, and estrangement, she sees how trauma shaped her. She realizes she hungered for love and, at the same time, yearned for distance. Her self-knowledge has broadened, and finally Lucy sees how class, gender, work, love, and silence contributed to her inevitable life. Now, she must engage in a narrative revision.

A Shift from Personal Fulfillment to Legacy

Erik Erikson, the child psychoanalyst who coined the phrase identity crisis, came up with the theory of psychosocial development, which describes the evolution of human beings throughout life stages. He claimed that individuals are always developing in relation to others: families, peers, partners, workplaces, communities, and society.

article continues after advertisement

Erikson identified the unique stage of midlife as a time when adults consider how their lives matter beyond personal success. This is what he calls generativity or stagnation. Generativity is the inclination to guide, nurture, create, mentor, contribute, and invest in something beyond the self. Stagnation, by contrast, is the painful sense of being stuck, unproductive, or disconnected from a larger purpose.

The key question, he says, is not only, “What have I achieved?” but also, “What am I giving to others and to the future?” Erikson suggests that the awakening of this period often includes a sharper sense that the self, which has been largely self-directed, must begin to consider legacy.

Finding Meaning in One’s Life Story

But the midlife awakening is much more than that. It is a reassessment or reevaluation of personal interactions and emotional regulation, emerging with a different orientation toward what matters most. In their 50s and 60s, many people no longer have the energy for chronic self-betrayal. They may have less time or patience for illusion or avoidance. Many discover they are less willing to over-explain, over-give, or people-please to maintain peace at any cost. In some ways, the awakening is a reallocation of emotional resources.

With their eyes opened, some see the relationships they once idealized differently. They also see themselves differently, as what they once called compassion they now see as enabling; what they once felt was loyalty they now recognize as fear; what they called love was actually duty.

Robert N. Butler, Pulitzer-Prize-winning geriatric psychiatrist and founder of the National Institute on Aging, identified this life stage in a 1962 article, “The Life Review: An Interpretation of Reminiscence in the Aged.” He theorized that older people, as they face mortality, are not simply nostalgic or reminiscing when they reflect on their lives.

Instead they are reorganizing their life story and finding meaning when they revisit memories, relationships, and achievements. They are reconciling painful experiences and moving toward acceptance or “ego integrity” — an older adult's ability to look back on their life with a sense of fulfillment and completeness. This stage, Butler wrote, "is characterized by the progressive return to consciousness of past experiences, and, particularly, the resurgence of unresolved conflicts; these are surveyed and reintegrated by the conscious mind."

article continues after advertisement

In their 50s and 60s, some gain an entirely new perspective on where they’ve been and where they’re going in the future. Less driven by obligation and momentum and more by intention, they forgive themselves, set boundaries, repair what can be repaired, and release what cannot be changed.

In midlife, they see again.

item.title: Corporate Change and the Power of Founding Stories
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Corporate Change and the Power of Founding Stories

How board directors can link past and future in the age of AI.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Founding stories help link disruptive change to a company’s honored legacy, reducing resistance.
  • Every company must now see itself as a technology company, regardless of its industry.
  • Boards should embed ongoing tech adaptation into culture, not treat it as a finite project.
  • Regular scenario planning helps Boards embrace uncertainty and prepare for peripheral threats.

In his classic novel about the French Revolution, Charles Dickens wrote, “It was the best of times. It was the worst of times.” (1975). That same quote also applies to the first half of the 21st Century. In this blog, we will focus on how Boards of Directors can meet today’s “Best of Times/Worst of Times” moment.

Our “Best of Times Worst of Times” Era

One one-hand, we are in the process of dramatic technological change through Artificial Intelligence, robotics, and emerging quantum computing systems. On the other hand, the United States is experiencing the decline of the middle class, a decline of national cohesion, and an increase in institutional mistrust. In an earlier Psychology Today blog, we discussed these issues in more detail (Stybel Peabody, 2024).

In A New Age of Reason, Larry Weber (2024) acknowledges both the best and worst of times but places emphasis on how corporate leaders can harness the positives. Mr. Weber is a national thought leader in corporate communications and founder of Racepoint Global.

From Farm Tractors to Agtech

The book contains Weber’s extensive interview with the CEO of Deere. This two-hundred-year-old company is known as a farm tractor company. The CEO and the Board have transformed Deere into an Agtech company whose mission is to empower farmers to do more with less.

A key lesson for Board Directors and CEOs is that to justify this new corporate mission, the CEO reached back into Deere’s founding story. Using the founding story as a jumping off point, he argued that Deere has always been in the business of transforming farming. Deere introduced the first steel plow in 1837. It replaced horse drawn tractors with engines in 1918.

By focusing on the founding story, companies help reduce internal resistance to change by linking disruptive change with honoring the company’s past.

Today, Deere leverages AI and computer vision with robotics and machine learning. Advanced sensors and robots place each seed with precision beyond human capacity. At the same time, it is reducing carbon emission. All these changes have benefited Deere’s net income and public reputation as a trustworthy resource to farmers.

Suggestions for Board Directors and CEOs

Every Company is a Technology Company. The author recounts working with General Motors’ introduction of Onstar. He told officials at GM, “You are no longer a car company. You are a technology company.” This concept also applies to professional service firms such as health care, education, and law.

article continues after advertisement

Keeping Up with Technology is Not a Project. Projects can be completed by certain dates. Technology is now a continuing component of corporate culture. Weber notes that Kodak missed the digital photography era and Intel missed the mobile phone wave because they were not keeping up with technology changes. Technological changes in the first quarter of the 21st Century will move faster than changes in the last quarter of the 20th Century.

Embrace Uncertainty in Structured Ways. We recommend that one hour a year of Board and C-Suite time be structured to focus on scenario planning around peripheral threats/opportunities. Management should be tasked with preparing ideas for Board discussion.

Vigilance is Paramount. Governmental and industry regulations are critical to minimize the damage new technologies can cause. The Board should be perceived by stakeholders as a vocal supporter of reasonable regulations. Being perceived as an institutional obstacle will only erode perceived institutional trust among stakeholders.

Create platforms for dialogue. Structure regular dialogue with adversaries through industry-standard setting committees. Take leadership roles in industry-wide standard setting committees. Ask marketing to arrange meetings with companies a year after they decided not to purchase your products/services. Use these meetings to gain more understanding of your company competitive strengths/weaknesses.

The Importance of Strategic Perspective

In the first quarter of the 21st century, Boards of Directors are thrust into another “Best of Times/Worst of Times” era. Managing the technological and social changes that will occur requires simultaneously reaching back to the company’s origin while structuring future Board agendas to ensure awareness of emerging threats/opportunities.

article continues after advertisement

It would be ideal for management to take the initiative and for the Board to be receptive. But we do not live in an ideal world. The typical corporate reward system tends to focus on quarterly and yearly goals. The consequence is a perceptual bias for tactical issues at the expense of strategic perspective.

item.title: Why Meaningful Coincidences Cluster During Life Changes
item.description:
Relationships

Why Meaningful Coincidences Cluster During Life Changes

How transition periods may amplify synchronicity.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Meaning arises from relationships, not isolated events.
  • Synchronicity is coherence across semi-independent systems.
  • Shared constraints can organize events without direct communication.
  • Coincidences can reveal hidden patterns in complex systems.

by Rob Sacco and Bernard Beitman

Most people have experienced it.

You think about someone you have not seen in years, and they call that afternoon. A stranger says exactly what you needed to hear during a difficult week. A chance encounter changes the direction of your career or relationship. The timing feels so improbable that it is difficult to dismiss as simple chance.

Carl Jung called these experiences synchronicities, meaningful coincidences that seem connected without an obvious causal explanation. Some people feel deeply spiritual. Others explain them as selective attention or confirmation bias. But perhaps there is another way to think about them.

One of the most striking features of synchronicity is that it rarely appears randomly across the lifespan. Meaningful coincidences often seem to cluster during periods of grief, illness, career change, divorce, retirement, becoming a parent, or other moments that reshape identity. Why might this happen? Several explanations have been proposed, ranging from changes in attention and pattern recognition to deeper processes of biological and psychological reorganization.

Synchronicity and Life Change

Person walking on a forest path at sunrise.
Source: Ewan Z Unsplash

Over many years of studying meaningful coincidences, we have noticed that they frequently arise during periods of emotional intensity, uncertainty, and major life transitions. These observations suggest that synchronicity is not an isolated curiosity but a surprisingly common human experience accompanying psychological change (Beitman, 2022).

Psychologists have long known that uncertainty changes perception. During unstable periods, people become more attentive to patterns, relationships, symbols, and unexpected connections that they might otherwise ignore. This heightened sensitivity undoubtedly explains part of the phenomenon. Yet there may be more occurring than changes in attention alone.

Developmental Timing and Reorganization

Recent research by colleagues and us has explored whether major psychological transitions themselves may follow preferred developmental timing patterns. Large epidemiological datasets suggest that the onset ages of several major mental disorders cluster around Fibonacci-derived harmonic intervals more often than expected by chance (Sacco, Beitman, and Marks-Tarlow, 2025).

During stable periods, biological, psychological, and social systems settle into established patterns. As instability and transformation increase, genetic, psychological, and environmental influences interact more strongly, making the system increasingly sensitive to small perturbations. This heightened sensitivity may create windows during which major psychological disorders are more likely to emerge. At the same time, increased openness and cognitive flexibility may enhance the perception and integration of meaningful coincidences. In this sense, psychopathology and synchronicity may represent different expressions of the same underlying process of reorganization.

article continues after advertisement

If these developmental windows reflect periods of increased plasticity, then the clustering of both disorder onset and synchronicity experiences near Fibonacci-derived ages may represent common transition points within human development. In this view, Fibonacci timing does not cause either mental illness or synchronicity. Rather, it may mark periods in which recursive developmental processes naturally concentrate transitions, increasing the probability of both adaptive and maladaptive outcomes.

The Inverted U of Synchronicity

An important qualification is that this relationship may not be linear. It may instead resemble an inverted U-shaped curve. Moderate levels of instability may maximize the ability to detect and integrate coherent patterns. As old assumptions loosen and new possibilities emerge, meaningful coincidences may be more likely to be recognized.

At the opposite extreme, however, excessive distress or cognitive disorganization may narrow attention and impair integration, reducing the ability to recognize broader patterns. In this sense, the same periods of heightened plasticity that increase vulnerability to psychopathology may also increase the probability of experiencing synchronicity, but only up to a point. Synchronicity may be most likely to emerge during periods of transformation that are sufficiently destabilizing to promote reorganization, but not so overwhelming that coherence collapses.

How Reorganization Creates Coincidence

The central mystery is not that coincidences occur. Coincidences happen frequently (Beitman, 2022). The question is why some of them become meaningful and why they seem to cluster during times of change. Periods of transition loosen routines. Relationships shift, old memories become active, and attention becomes tuned toward possibilities that were previously ignored.

Meanwhile, the external world continues evolving. Families, workplaces, friendships, and social environments are all changing simultaneously. Small changes occurring at one level ripple into others. New conversations take place. Chance encounters become possible. Different decisions place people in different places at different times.

article continues after advertisement

As internal and external systems reorganize together, events that would ordinarily remain disconnected may temporarily intersect. Meaningful coincidences may therefore represent moments when multiple processes align across different scales of life.

Complex systems researchers often observe similar behavior near periods of transition. Small changes can produce unexpectedly large effects because the entire system has become more sensitive. Fractal systems provide a useful framework because similar patterns can emerge simultaneously across different scales. Thoughts, emotions, relationships, habits, and social environments may all undergo parallel forms of change during transition, temporarily increasing the probability that previously independent events converge into meaningful alignments.

In this sense, synchronicity may be less about isolated events and more about temporary episodes of multiscale coherence. The coincidence itself may simply be the visible expression of a deeper process of reorganization.

A Middle Ground

This perspective offers a middle ground between mystical certainty and skeptical dismissal. Meaningful coincidences need not be messages sent by the universe. Nor must they be reduced to cognitive mistakes. They may instead reflect the remarkable capacity of complex human systems to generate coherence during periods of transformation.

Research into meaningful coincidences remains in its early stages. Although many questions remain unanswered, one observation appears consistent: Life transitions often coincide with periods of heightened meaning and unexpected connections.

Comment

The next time an unlikely coincidence appears during a major life change, it may be worth asking: What is reorganizing within my life that made this moment possible?

Perhaps synchronicity is neither magic nor illusion. Perhaps it is what coherence feels like from the inside when life is reorganizing itself.

item.title: Trade Screen Time for a Creative Hobby
item.description:
Creativity

Trade Screen Time for a Creative Hobby

Creative hobbies boost mood, confidence, connection, and mental health.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Creative hobbies can reduce stress, anxiety, and depression while boosting well-being.
  • Making things builds skills, confidence, and self-esteem in ways passive leisure cannot.
  • Social hobbies such as improv can strengthen connection, communication, and empathy.
  • Even small amounts of creative time can improve mood and mental health.

Last weekend on stage, I pretended to be a live and sentient pot of chili with my improv class during a show about finding love in quick-service restaurants. Lots of laughs for it, and it was also a chance to do an activity I love with a group of good friends.

I’ve been doing improv for over a year, and I’m now performing on two teams in Chicago. It’s a fun hobby, on top of some other pastimes I have: Woodworking, bodybuilding, and making electronic dance music.

Obviously, I’m a hobby aficionado, but even just one creative hobby can bring more energy, enjoyment, and generative energy to life.

What Creative Hobbies Do for Your Brain

People wonder how they could add one more thing to their lives. But the most common American hobby is watching TV (the average American adult spends almost 4 hours a day passively watching TV). Unfortunately, high rates of TV watching, especially for people watching solo, are linked to being sedentary, increased consumption of ultra-processed foods, loneliness, and more.

As a therapist, I’ve noted that many patients feel like their busy lives don’t include much that’s about themselves. They feel like they’re tossed back and forth between work obligations, fights with their siblings, and their own negative mental self-talk.

Generative hobbies—hobbies where you actively make something, rather than passively consume something—help us to develop our personalities by defining and acting on our interests and building a skill in something. Not coincidentally, building skill is the foundation of self-esteem. Even better, social hobbies (like improv–or any other activity you do as part of a group) help to build social connections–something every therapist knows most people feel like they are lacking.

In leisure studies (yes, this is an academic field!), hobbies are divided into “casual leisure”—watching TV, eating, and the like–and “serious leisure”—basically any pastime where we’re engaged and creating something, and especially where we’re learning or using even a little bit of special skill, knowledge, or experience.

Generative hobbies range from solitary activities at home (think knitting, painting, or building model airplanes) to hobbies that take you far afield, like improv. They can include activities that might be pricey, like amateur astronomy, or that can cost almost nothing, like creative writing.

Hobbies have enormous benefits. They can help to alleviate depression, anxiety, and stress. Hobbies that involve physical activity, like yoga, weightlifting, or running, provide an enormous range of benefits to mental and physical health.

article continues after advertisement

In a study of over 1,000 German hobby musicians, engaging with their hobby each day was linked to both positive affect and feelings of competence. And hobbies don’t have to be complex and involved to be helpful. In a study of 100 women university students in New Zealand, doing a daily coloring activity, compared to a logic puzzle control group, was linked with lower depression and anxiety. These positive benefits come from actively exploring our interests and values and then acting on them (a core aspect of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy), building a skill (the foundation of self-esteem), and connecting with other people (increasing and strengthening social connections and support).

Some hobbies (like improv) are more involved and might require big steps out of a person’s comfort zone. But there’s evidence that those big risks can bring big rewards. A meta-analysis of 21 research studies including over 4,000 participants indicated that theater training participation was linked with improved understanding of others, social communication, and social interaction skills, which the authors attributed to the performers being required to learn to express themselves, enhance their verbal and non-verbal communication skills, and work with others to produce a final product, all as part of their theater training.

How Do We Find New Hobbies?

First, look back at what brought you joy in childhood or adolescence. Did you love drawing or painting as a kid? Order some supplies online and see if that still brings you joy.

Second, is there an interest you always wanted to try, but never got to pursue? Maybe you were interested in the stars and space, but lived in a light-polluted city? Or maybe you dreamed of acting, but grew up in a small town with no community theater? As an adult, you might have more opportunities to reignite those interests.

Third, try something entirely new. When I started improv, I had no theater background beyond two high school drama productions. As an adult, I’ve loved comedy podcasts like Comedy Bang Bang and This Book Changed My Life, which exposed me to improv. And hearing interviews with Tina Fey and Amy Poehler taught me about the philosophy of improv: Build something with your friends and have fun. That kicked off my interest, and I’m now on stage in two shows a week.

Overcoming Barriers

Of course, we’re all tired, broke, and distracted—so, picking up a new hobby, especially one requiring more effort than watching Netflix, can seem like unrealistic advice, or just one more thing on our to-do list.

Hobbies cost money, they take time, and we don’t know anyone else who’s intrigued by our interests…the list of barriers can seem daunting. But we don't have to invest in top-quality supplies or equipment. Thrift stores, online swap sites, and other hobbyists can help equip you for little money. As for time, since we’re not looking to become an expert, you don't need those 10,000 hours. And as for learning or community, YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram can be sources of inspiration, offering content made by hobbyists who would love to share their interests with you.

article continues after advertisement

We’re losing pastimes and hobbies, where we can be creative and stretch ourselves, to passive activities like streaming shows and movies. But the barriers to starting up a new hobby don’t have to be high, and the benefits can be enormous. Those shows are going to be there forever, but you can find a way to get on the road to playing a living pot of chili on a stage in front of dozens of people today.

item.title: AI, the Chip and the Good-Enough Clinical Question
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI, the Chip and the Good-Enough Clinical Question

What Butterfly Network and Midjourney are asking medicine to reconsider.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Midjourney and Butterfly Network are asking how much resolution medicine actually needs.
  • The chip array and the AI create a new way to see inside the body.
  • A spa scan called a side-effect could reshape who sees your body first, and why.
Source: Image by efes from Pixabay.

Nobody saw this coming, at least I didn't. Midjourney, the company built on generating images that never existed is now trying to generate images of what's actually inside you.

The partnership with Butterfly Network feels a bit strange until you look at the underlying technical problem of turning terabytes of sound wave data into a clinically useful 3D image of the human body. It's structurally close to what Midjourney's currently does, but a different domain—one that is both essential and lucrative.

A Century-Old Assumption

Medical imaging has generally operated on the premise that better pictures make better medicine. X-rays gave way to CT. CT gave way to MRI. Each generation delivered finer and more appropriate anatomical detail. From this basis emerged the clinical confidence that diagnostic truth lived somewhere at the far end of a resolution curve.

Butterfly Network may be challenging that premise from the ground up. Thousands of ultrasound-on-chip transducers make possible a kind of sensing that conventional imaging doesn't provide.

What the Tech Changes

Butterfly's ultrasound-on-chip moves transducer manufacturing onto semiconductor silicon and that's the same methodology that produces processors. That density changes the game. The company reports half a million sensors, each about the size of a grain of sand, generating terabytes of data per second. The resulting image isn't just captured but reconstructed with artificial intelligence.

The Resolution Threshold

Medicine has, in many cases, used resolution as a proxy for certainty. The sharper the image, the more we know. The more we know, the better we decide. But resolution and knowledge aren't the same thing, and treating them as interchangeable has real costs including radiation, time, and the unnecessary use of high resolution imaging.

What Butterfly may be introducing, perhaps without fully framing it this way, is a resolution threshold. Not the highest possible resolution, but one that's sufficient to answer the question actually being asked. Is there something here worth looking at more closely? If not, we're done. If yes, now we order the MRI. That logic already exists in good clinical practice. What's new is that it could exist at population scale, outside the clinic, before symptoms appear.

article continues after advertisement

The Stethoscope Didn't Replace Anything

When Laennec used a simple cylinder and pressed it to a patient's chest in 1816, he didn't replace anything. His stethoscope became a new early step into the physical exam. Butterfly's scanner, if it develops as imagined, does something similar and arrives earlier in the diagnostic sequence. It asks, first, whether anything here is worth a closer look. That makes expensive, high-resolution imaging more selective rather than more routine.

The Scan Becomes a Side-Effect

The first planned Midjourney Spa in San Francisco will have the usual hot tubs and saunas and what the announcement calls "pools of golden light which softly scan your body." The scans, they say, are a side-effect, an interesting word choice, given that side-effects are usually what we're trying to avoid.

What they mean, perhaps, is incidental. Simply put, you go for the water and the data follows. That repositioning of imaging as an "ambient experience" rather than clinical encounter is curiously new territory. The fluorescent light, the paper gown, even the psychological discomfort all reflect what has always been part of the diagnostic contract. Midjourney is proposing to dissolve that contract and replace dread with warm water.

Whether that's progress depends on questions the announcement doesn't raise. A person who barely thinks about the scan may also barely think about what comes back from it. The resolution threshold isn't only a technical setting. It also might be psychological one.

The Image Is Still Blurry

The prototype currently takes twenty minutes, not sixty seconds. Roughly twelve people have been scanned. The FDA pathway, if taken, is long and the San Francisco spa doesn't open until 2027. Medicine has seen compelling concepts arrive well ahead of their evidence, and this one is no exception.

The image is sharp enough to see something worth watching. For me, it isn't sharp enough yet to know exactly what it is.

item.title: A World Beyond Erotic Excitement
item.description:
Sex

A World Beyond Erotic Excitement

Improve women’s mental health and relieve depression and pain.

Posted July 1, 2026

Listen carefully. That faint buzzing you hear just might be the woman—or couple—next door enjoying one or more vibrators. Today, more than half of adult American women own at least one. Only a fraction of couples include them in partner lovemaking, but that fraction is growing.

Vibrators do more than help women have orgasms. A recent study shows that it also improves users’ sexual and mental health. Los Angeles researchers recruited 53 cisgender women aged 19 to 80, with an average age of 55, who consulted at the Cedars-Sinai Medical Center. The researchers used standard questionnaires to assess the women’s sexual health and function. Then the researchers gave participants small “bullet” multi-speed vibrators and instructed them to apply them to their vulvas for five to 10 minutes, two to three times a week for three months, at which point the researchers re-assessed them.

Their sexual function, that is, their responsiveness to genital play, improved (p = 0.002). Their sexual pain scores decreased (p = 0.0008). In older women, vaginal atrophy, painful thinning of the vaginal lining, also decreased (p = 0.018). And those who were depressed at the start of the study experienced relief (p = 0.011). The researchers concluded: “Vibrator use was associated with improved sexual, genitourinary, and mental health.”

Increasingly Popular Among Women

Indiana University researchers surveyed a representative sample of 3,800 adult American women. More than half (53 percent) owned at least one vibrator (lifetime use). Three-quarters agreed that vibrators:

  • Are a healthy part of women’s sexuality.
  • Add excitement and enhance partner sex.
  • Facilitate orgasms.
  • Two-thirds agreed that vibes reduce pressure on partners to bring users to orgasm.

Increasingly Popular in Partner Lovemaking with Men

In another study, Indiana University investigators interviewed 1,047 adult men. Forty-five percent said they’d been involved in partner vibrator play at least once; 10 percent frequently. Men who included vibrators regularly in partner lovemaking reported more desire, firmer erections, better orgasms, happier lovers, and greater satisfaction.

In the Indiana poll, the majority of men agreed that vibrators:

  • Are a healthy part of women’s sexuality.
  • Enhance partner sex.
  • Facilitate women’s orgasms.

The Myths Are Fading Fast

Unfortunately, some people of all genders continue to struggle with lingering myths about vibrators:

Myth: Vibrators are for lonely losers.

Truth: Actually, single women are less likely to use them than married women. Compared with singles, married women usually have more regular sex. They think about it more and are more likely to use vibrators.

Myth: If women need vibrators to climax, something is wrong with them. Truth: No. They’re normal. Some women just need more stimulation than fingers or tongues provide.

article continues after advertisement

Myth: If women need vibrators to orgasm, their men are lousy lovers. Truth: Possibly, but not necessarily. Even when men provide what most women prefer—leisurely, playful, whole-body lovemaking with lots of cunnilingus—many perfectly normal women need vibrators to climax.

Myth: Vibrators replace men. Truth. No. Vibrators provide only one thing: intense stimulation. They don’t smile, converse, kiss, embrace, warm the bed, tell jokes, say I love you, or share women’s joys and heartaches.

Myth: Vibrators ruin women for sex without them. Truth: Does driving ruin you for walking? No, it just gets you there faster. It's the same for vibrators; they don’t change the body’s ability to respond to other caresses.

Myth: Vibrators are addictive. Truth: Some women become very fond of vibrators. But they are not addictive. Over time, as these devices teach women about the full range of their erotic responsiveness, many find it takes less vibrator stimulation to get the job done.

Myth: Vibrators numb the genitals. Truth: Possibly. In the Indiana survey, 11 percent of users reported occasional numbness. If this occurs, use lubricant, press less, or try a lower-power vibe.

Myth: Vibrators cause urinary tract infections. Truth: Vibrators don’t cause UTIs, but using them carelessly might. If vibes touch the anal area, they may pick up UTI-causing bacteria. After any anal vibrator play, wash the devices before they are used.

Which Type Is Best?

There is no “best” vibrator, and marketers offer large selections.

  • Some look like erections. Others are more abstract cylinders. Some have flat tips; others are pancake-shaped.
  • Some are battery-powered. Others plug in. The former can be used anywhere; the latter is more powerful.
  • Sizes vary. Small ones are good for travel.
  • Dual-action vibrators have small protrusions extending from their shafts.
  • Materials include hard or soft plastic, jelly (like gummy candies), or plastics that feel like skin.
  • Some vibrators have only one speed, others several, allowing a range of sensation.
  • Most vibrators are not waterproof. If you’d like to use them in tubs, showers, or swimming pools, buy a waterproof model. Their electrical components are sealed inside their housings.
  • “Kits” include basic cylindrical vibrators and attachments that alter their look and the sensations they produce.
  • Most battery-powered ones are not designed to operate continuously for more than 20 minutes at low speeds and 10 minutes at high speeds. Plug-in models can run much longer.
  • The clitoris can be very sensitive to touch. During partner vibe play, many women insist on handling them themselves. But most women appreciate being held, kissed, caressed, and encouraged to enjoy themselves.

item.title: When What You’re Told Conflicts With What You See
item.description:
Cognitive Dissonance

When What You’re Told Conflicts With What You See

How does cognitive dissonance help us make sense of conflicting 'truths'?

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Cognitive dissonance occurs when we're told something that conflicts with our own observations.
  • Responses include trusting your own perception, choosing to accept what others tell you, or disengaging.
  • Choosing to speak up in conflicting situations reinforces a norm of prosocial intervention.

"The Party told you to reject the evidence of your eyes and ears. It was their final, most essential command." — George Orwell

Imagine watching someone on TV, perhaps a public figure, expert, or politician, make a confident claim about an event or situation that you witnessed for yourself. You’ve watched the footage, followed the reporting, or directly observed what happened. Yet the account you’re given contradicts what you believe you have clearly seen and heard. This scenario raises an important question: What do you do when those in positions of authority or influence ask you to doubt the evidence of your own eyes and ears?

The Psychology of ‘Don’t Believe Your Own Eyes’

Being told to reject what we see and hear creates a powerful form of psychological tension called cognitive dissonance. This is when the external messages we receive conflict with our own lived experience and perception of the world. Festinger’s (1957) cognitive dissonance theory suggests that, in order to feel that the world makes sense, we seek harmony between our beliefs and attitudes, and will avoid disharmony wherever possible.

The real challenge comes when we’re faced with two statements that are clearly incompatible such as, ‘I heard a politician make a specific campaign promise’ and ‘the politician now claims that they never made that promise’.

When this happens, we have a few options. The first is to trust your own perception, and the evidence of your own eyes and ears. Alternatively, you can accept the narrative that you’ve been given by others, even though it’s inconsistent with your own perception. Al Marrar & Allevato (2022) found that cognitive dissonance can affect what information people attend to and remember, particularly in relation to politics. Their research suggested that if what a politician was saying didn’t match what participants had witnessed themselves, they dealt with the inconsistency through selective recall of information. In other words, ignorance offers more than just bliss; it also provides cognitive consistency.

Another way we can deal with cognitive dissonance is to simply disengage from the issue, allowing us to remain uncertain about what is true and avoid having to challenge either inconsistent belief. When the truth feels unclear or is socially contested, people are far less likely to challenge it. It can be argued that those who take this option are withdrawing from discomfort rather than genuinely being unsure about what the truth is. Rosa (2024) suggested that we are all capable of knowing the logical truth about important issues, and that it is irrational to believe otherwise. Disengagement from the discussion therefore reflects a desire not to get involved rather than an inability to know what is true.

Why It Matters

Harm rarely begins at its most extreme point. It blooms in environments where discrepancies go unchallenged. Doing nothing in a conflicting situation is not a neutral act. It can suggest that the issue doesn’t matter, or that asking questions to get to the truth is discouraged. Opting to disengage or ignoring key information helps to establish social norms around what is acceptable, what should be contested, and what can go unchallenged. We see this in everything from workplace misconduct to public discourse, where small acts of non-intervention can accumulate, creating pathways for more significant harm.

article continues after advertisement

However, even one dissenting voice can encourage people to ask questions, consider what they know to be true, and carefully reflect on the issue at hand rather than disengaging from it. Obermaier & Schmid (2026) found that choosing to speak up in conflicting situations reinforces the perceived norm for prosocial intervention in those around us and, in turn, increases individuals’ sense of personal responsibility.

Continuing to speak up and share what you believe to be true disrupts false consensus and ensures that silence and disengagement don’t become the norm. It also reduces the likelihood of pluralistic ignorance, where people assume that everyone else agrees simply because they’re not speaking out to challenge a situation. Speaking out doesn’t have to be extreme or confrontational. It can be as simple as saying ‘that’s not what I saw’, ‘I’m not sure that’s right’, or even ‘can we check that?’

So, stay curious. Ask questions. Check what you’ve seen. Because once we stop questioning, it becomes far easier to just accept what we’re told, whether it’s true or not.

item.title: The Book Is the Boss for a Writer of Immense Imagination
item.description:
Creativity

The Book Is the Boss for a Writer of Immense Imagination

Not knowing where you’ll end up makes the story you’re writing more compelling.

Posted July 1, 2026

Fun with interlocking stories.
Source: Susan K. Perry

A bit like one of those Russian nested dolls, Guillermo Stitch's latest novel keeps surprising the reader. Stories within stories take the forms of science fiction, mystery, and more, all blending and bleeding together in unexpected ways.

Curious about Stitch's writing process for such a demanding project, I asked him a few questions and he responded between flights on his European book tour.

Susan K. Perry: Your newest book, The Coast of Everything, is 747 pages long, and I wonder how many revisions it went through. Many writers seem to think that one or two revisions are plenty. I have to suppose that your publisher weighed in.

Guillermo Stitch: The editorial process for the book was complex, making this question difficult to answer. There were editorial sweeps on each narrative element of the book (there are five, arguably six, distinct elements or strands) both during that element’s writing and upon its completion.

This involved trusted readers alongside me—some constants but also some new readers chosen each time for compatibility with genre.

Certainly there were major cuts over the years. But additions too—it was necessary to approach each part as a fiction that could stand on its own two feet but also as a body part in a larger organism, and that is actually a contradiction, creating two separate and conflicting sets of editorial criteria.

The more straightforward set was, let’s say, modular in nature—it concerned the need to whip each tale into its own best shape: the fairly traditional business of cutting and correcting. The other set had to concern itself with allowing these narrative elements to bleed, or grow, into each other. This was more nebulous, mysterious and unpredictable. Stories want to grow into each other so it’s largely a question of just letting them—but at times surgery is required. There can be scar tissue—increased word count.

It makes little sense in my process to talk about the number of revisions—I am incapable of opening the file without making changes. Hundreds. By the time my publisher and editor saw the complete manuscript, it was less a question of line editing (although there was certainly some to be done) and more a question of decision-making. Should we mitigate this property of the book? Accentuate that property? 747 pages is where we ended up—the book’s best self.

Quit? Never.

SKP: Were there points during the writing of this book when you felt like quitting?

GS: No, I don’t experience this. I consider myself in service to the work, not it to me. If I can’t even complete it, what is the point of me?

My moments of self-doubt are more likely to arise between books, when I’m not writing and there is the temptation to consider extraneous, real-world factors that are invariably unfavorable—that most people don’t read fiction, that most people who do read fiction don’t read literary fiction, that most people who do read literary fiction don’t read the innovative or experimental, that most people who do read the innovative and experimental don’t like long books.

It’s difficult to think of a single positive motivation for doing what I do. Fortunately, positive motivation is unnecessary—I keep going because there is simply nothing else to do.

Details, Details...

SKP: You’ve written that you hadn’t worked out the details of The Coast of Everything until you were “at the finish line.” Can you describe a little of your creative writing process?

GS: I hadn’t worked out all of the details. The final piece placed in a jigsaw puzzle can be the first to reveal the image. I used no bulletin board, no diagrams, occasionally a list. No software.

It’s crucial to me that everything swills around in my head—it’s a soup in there, a witch’s brew. It’s a messy and unreliable way of going about things, which suits me just fine.

SKP: Dare I ask if you’ve got another novel in mind?

GS: Yes, I’ll start work on a novel presently. I don’t know much about it yet, but it will be set in a barrel of sherry.

item.title: Do Birds of a Feather Prefer to Flock Together?
item.description:
Friends

Do Birds of a Feather Prefer to Flock Together?

The friends we want aren't the friends we get.

Posted July 1, 2026

Key points
  • Similarity breeds friendship formation, stability, and decreased dissolution.
  • Two opposing hypotheses are the homophily-selection hypothesis and the default-selection hypothesis.
  • These findings can be explained by evolutionary processes.

I’ll admit it. I was a nerd in elementary school.

I don’t mean that I was smarter than the other kids. I mean that my primary social crowd was “the nerds.”

And—no—peer crowd labels like “the nerds,” “the jocks,” and “the populars” aren’t made-up constructs reserved for catty teen movies. Although labels and categories can change through generations (Crabbe and colleagues, 2021), peer crowds exist. They are especially prominent in adolescence and can negatively influence teens in lower-status social crowds.

Source: Alexander Mass / Pexels

For example, Helms and colleagues (2014) found that although teens in higher-status social crowds (populars and jocks) did not significantly differ in most risky behaviors compared with those in lower-status social crowds (brains and burnouts), teens who assumed high-status peers engaged in substance use showed steeper increases in their own substance use from grades nine to eleven.

Even adults are identified by specific attributes that are associated with different levels of status. Adults looking for romantic partners tend to prioritize physical attractiveness or earning potential. They want these ideals to be present in their future mates—or at least they say they do. Eastwick and Finkel (2008) studied romantic partners before and after speed dating. Before speed dating started, participants tended to identify physical attractiveness and earning prospects as attributes they’d look for in a mate. But these preferences, identified at the beginning of the speed dating event, failed to predict the characteristics of the people they ended up with one month later.

Did I prefer to be friends with the nerds? Honestly, no.

But since we’re all friends here, I’ll also admit to lying awake in bed past my bedtime—praying that I could one day infiltrate the popular group. Does this sound desperate? Maybe. Did my wish come true? Sadly, no. But guess what? I was far from being the only one who thought that way, apparently.

Research focusing on similarity in friendships and romantic relationships has made three things apparent:

  1. Our friends are similar to us
  2. We become even more similar to our friends over time
  3. Similarity contributes to stability while dissimilarity leads to dissolution (friendships ending; Laursen, 2017)
article continues after advertisement

Clearly, there is truth to the saying, “birds of a feather flock together.” We end up with similar others.

But is this because we actively choose friends who are similar to us? If we were asked whom we really, genuinely, actually wanted to befriend, whom would we choose?

Source: Hobi Photography / Pixels

There are two opposing hypotheses to address this question (Sijtsema and colleagues, 2010): The homophily-selection hypothesis assumes that we end up befriending similar others because we actively seek out similar people as friends. Conversely, the default-selection hypothesis posits that people tend to reach up when it comes to friendship, but end up with similar others by default. They aim to befriend someone who is “better” than they are—someone who has more desirable attributes than they do—someone who is of higher status. Regardless, they end up with someone who resembles them in these attributes.

Which is it? Do we seek out similar others as friends, or do we want something different?

This question inspired my coauthored research paper, recently published in The Journal of Social and Personal Relationships (Sherrod, Selover, Kahn, Kaniusonyte, and Laursen, 2026). Two longitudinal studies included a total of 725 children aged 10-14 living in the U.S. or Lithuania. We asked children to nominate and rank their friends and their desired friends (whom they would like to befriend).

Children were considered friends when nominations were reciprocal. For example, if you chose Betty as your friend and Betty chose you too, that would be a reciprocal friendship. Desired friendship was measured by asking children whom they would want as friends (someone who isn’t already one of their friends).

Children also nominated classmates on academic achievement, attractiveness, athleticism, fun, popularity, and unpopularity. First, we found that only about 3 to 13 percent of desired friends became actual (reciprocal) friends by the end of the school year. Therefore, most children did not end up becoming friends with the classmates they wanted to befriend.

We also found that children nominated as desired friends tended to have higher status and more favorable attributes (higher scores on popularity, fun, athleticism, attractiveness, and academic achievement) than children who were not picked as desired friends. Moreover, when we compared desired friends to their nominators (the children who picked them), desired friends scored higher on ideal attributes. Children were significantly more similar to their reciprocal friends than they were to their desired friends.

What does this mean for us?

Our findings, along with earlier research on friendship and dating, suggest that although birds of a feather flock together, they seem to prefer different company (at least, at the start). If this feels deflating to you, well, welcome to reality.

I, for one, felt validated in my own relationship experiences when these research findings came to light. When taking a step back, the default-selection hypothesis makes a whole lot of sense evolutionarily. Of course, we reach for higher-value targets. And, of course, we usually end up with similar others.

Consider social exchange theory, which posits that relationships form, last, or end because humans engage in a continuous cost-benefit analysis. At first, we want the shiny, bright fruit that is out of reach, but once we recognize that we are giving more than we are receiving, we reach for (and appreciate) the fruit at eye level. Arguably, it is better to reach for the higher-hanging fruit first, just in case (you may end up in that 3 to 13 percent based on our study).

It is also adaptive to be somewhat delusional in our own self-perceptions. Research focusing on depression shows that happier people tend to overestimate their abilities and the probability of positive outcomes. Conversely, people who are moderately depressed tend to view the world and themselves more realistically. This has been called “depressive realism” (Garrett and colleagues, 2014).

The moral of the story is this: It may help us to be slightly delusional in our optimism. Go for it. Reach for the stars. Take a shot at that relationship. At the same time, if the relationship partners you end up with are different from what you hoped for—you’re in good company—and are only human after all.
